facts.fact: OpenCV's solvePnP documentation credits its SOLVEPNP_EPNP method to Moreno-Noguer, Lepetit and Fua (the EPnP paper), and describes EPnP as a non-iterative solution to the general PnP problem for n >= 4 points.
OpenCV 4.x documentation (as reported in a search snippet, not verified on the page) states the SOLVEPNP_DLS flag is a broken implementation and falls back to EPnP.

The Bengal-HP_RU head-pose dataset paper uses six 2D facial landmarks (nose tip, chin, eye corners, mouth corners) matched to a canonical 3D face model and calls solvePnP, assuming a pinhole camera with focal length set to the image width and principal point at the image center (approximation, not calibrated).
A 2022 face-reconstruction paper states intrinsic parameters K can be obtained through an off-line calibration step, after which solvePnP is used with known 2D-3D correspondences.
PnP methods assume landmark coordinates are free of lens distortion; distorted landmarks must be undistorted first (per a search snippet from OpenCV-related material).

Practitioner sources (photography blogs, snippet-level) state that for a fixed camera-to-subject distance, a normal and a wide-angle or telephoto lens produce the same linear perspective on the face; facial distortion is driven mainly by camera distance rather than focal length alone.

Different focal lengths require different subject distances to keep subject size constant, so changing focal length indirectly changes face perspective; the search snippets report that short lenses force close distances and make wide-angle portraits look worst.
Photography guidance (snippet-level, practitioner) recommends holding a phone at arm's length for selfies to reduce face distortion.

A study reported in search snippets found that photos taken at 50 mm focal length were rated as significantly less feminine/masculine, attractive, and dominant than images taken at longer focal lengths; the exact source article was not identified in the snippet, so the sample size is unconfirmed.
Two orthogonal vanishing points are the minimum needed to calibrate a traffic camera's focal length in one cited paper, which gives a closed-form relation for focal length from them.
A pose-estimation paper (snippet-level) states at least three vanishing points are needed to estimate pose, and at least four are needed if focal length is estimated simultaneously.
The BLAM Blender calibration add-on has been discontinued by its maintainers, who direct users to fSpy; BLAM's single-vanishing-point mode computes camera orientation from a known focal length.
No fSpy documentation or algorithm description was found in search results; fSpy-specific workflow claims remain unverified.
The cvlab multiview_calib tool estimates each camera's intrinsics separately with OpenCV's calibration framework, then computes extrinsics linearly and refines them with bundle adjustment.

Marginalized Bundle Adjustment (2026 arXiv) jointly optimizes per-camera intrinsics K_i and extrinsics P_i from unordered RGB frames, initializing intrinsics from a DUSt3R pointmap when calibration is unknown.
A patent snippet notes that camera parameters and 3D points may fail to converge in bundle adjustment because of accumulated error, even after BA is applied.
Generalized Procrustes analysis removes rotation, translation and uniform scale before statistical shape modelling of 3D faces, repeatedly aligning each shape to the recomputed mean shape.
A 3D face paper (arXiv 1708.06703) aligns faces by translation and rotation only and does not factor out scale, evaluating surface error after Procrustes alignment.

A face frontalization paper parameterizes face pose as scale, rotation and translation mapping a face-centered frame to the camera frame, and fits a 3DMM to 2D/3D landmarks by scaling, rotating and translating the model.
A 2026 facial-movement study uses Procrustes with translation, rotation and anisotropic scaling, which differs from uniform-scale similarity alignment.

contradictions: Shape-model practice differs on scale: GPA-style pipelines (arXiv 1209.6491) remove uniform scale, while arXiv 1708.06703 keeps scale out of alignment and pose fitting (arXiv 2010.13676) fits scale as a parameter. Not a hard contradiction, but the handling of scale is inconsistent across sources.
Bengal-HP_RU sets focal length to image width (an approximation), whereas the 2022 face reconstruction paper calls for offline calibration of K; the two approaches conflict for uncalibrated photos.

Photography sources attribute face distortion mainly to camera distance, while a study snippet attributes perceived differences to focal length (50 mm vs longer); these are consistent only if focal length is read as a proxy for distance.
